issues.legal_issue: The time limit for making an award applies to an emergency acquisition after possession has been taken and the land has vested in the State.
material_facts: Possession was taken under the emergency acquisition procedure before an award was made, and the land thereby vested in the State.
The award was made more than two years after the declaration.
issues.conclusion: Justice Swatanter Kumar held that the time limit for making an award does not apply to an acquisition under the emergency procedure once possession has been taken and the land has vested. Justice Asok Kumar Ganguly disagreed with the approach that would treat possession as valid despite non-compliance with the advance-payment safeguard. The judges differed, and the matter was referred to a larger Bench; this issue was not resolved by a binding majority ruling.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Swatanter Kumar relied on Sections 11A, 16, 17(1), 17(3A), 17(3B), and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. He applied the three-Judge Bench ruling in Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P., followed in Awadh Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar, P. Chinnanna v. State of A.P., Pratap v. State of Rajasthan, and Allahabad Development Authority v. Nasiruzzaman, and referred to Offshore Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Bangalore Development Authority. He distinguished Yusufbhai Noormohmed Nendoliya v. State of Gujarat as addressing calculation of the period excluded by a court stay, not the application of the award deadline to emergency acquisitions. Justice Ganguly considered the earlier discussion in Satendra Prasad Jain on non-payment unnecessary to its result and not binding on that point.

predicates.emergency_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked an emergency procedure.
predicates.possession_taken_before_award: The acquiring authority took possession before making the award.
predicates.land_vested_in_state: The land was treated as having vested in the State after possession was taken.

issues.definition: When an emergency-acquisition case involves possession before the award and the land is treated as vested in the State, the award deadline does not cause the acquisition to lapse under Justice Swatanter Kumar's view.

issues.legal_issue: Payment of the prescribed advance compensation is a condition precedent to taking possession and vesting land under the emergency acquisition procedure.
material_facts: The land was acquired under the emergency procedure and possession was taken before an award was made.
The landowners were not paid the prescribed portion of the estimated compensation before possession was taken.
The beneficiary said it had deposited funds with State authorities, but the landowners had not received the advance compensation before possession.
issues.conclusion: Justice Asok Kumar Ganguly held that the advance-payment requirement is mandatory and a condition precedent to valid possession and vesting; without compliance, taking possession is illegal and vesting does not occur. Justice Swatanter Kumar held that non-compliance does not invalidate the acquisition or undo vesting, although the payment obligation remains. The judges differed, and the matter was referred to a larger Bench; neither position was resolved by a binding majority ruling.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Ganguly relied on Sections 17(1), 17(2), 17(3A), and 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and Article 300A of the Constitution. He applied strict construction of expropriatory legislation, reading the emergency-acquisition provisions as a composite scheme, and relied on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, Gujarat Electricity Board v. Girdharlal Motilal, Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. Darius Shapur Chenai, and Bharat Petroleum Corporation v. Maddula Ratnavalli. He rejected the contrary observation in Satendra Prasad Jain as unnecessary to that case and, alternatively, contrary to the statute. Justice Kumar relied on the absence of an express statutory consequence for default, the vesting scheme, and Satendra Prasad Jain and Tika Ram v. State of U.P. for the view that default does not invalidate the acquisition.

predicates.emergency_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked an emergency procedure.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the land.
predicates.advance_compensation_received_before_pos: The landowners received the prescribed advance compensation before possession was taken.

issues.definition: In an emergency-acquisition case, if possession is taken before the landowners receive the prescribed advance compensation, Justice Ganguly's view is that the possession is illegal and the State acquires no vesting.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to pay advance compensation before taking possession invalidates the emergency acquisition.
material_facts: Possession was taken under the emergency procedure before an award was made.
The landowners had not received the prescribed advance compensation before possession was taken.
The Act did not specify that non-payment would cause the acquisition to lapse or become invalid.
issues.conclusion: Justice Swatanter Kumar held that non-payment does not invalidate or cause the acquisition to lapse after possession and vesting, though the payment obligation remains. Justice Asok Kumar Ganguly held that non-payment makes the taking of possession illegal and prevents vesting. The judges differed, and the matter was referred to a larger Bench; this issue was not resolved by a binding majority ruling.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Kumar applied Sections 17(1), 17(3A), 17(3B), and 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, reasoning that the Legislature specified no lapse or invalidity consequence for default and that a court should not add one. He relied on Satendra Prasad Jain, Tika Ram, and Pratap v. State of Rajasthan. Justice Ganguly applied Sections 17(1), 17(2), and 17(3A), read with Article 300A, as imposing a mandatory condition precedent, and relied on the principles of strict construction in expropriatory legislation and due process described in Maneka Gandhi and R.C. Cooper.

predicates.emergency_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked an emergency procedure.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the land.
predicates.advance_compensation_received_before_pos: The landowners received the prescribed advance compensation before possession was taken.

issues.definition: In an emergency-acquisition case, if possession is taken before the landowners receive the prescribed advance compensation, Justice Kumar's view is that the acquisition remains valid despite the payment default.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner deprived of advance compensation in an emergency acquisition is entitled to additional interest for the delay in payment.
material_facts: Possession was taken under the emergency procedure before the prescribed advance compensation was received by the landowners.
Funds had been deposited by the beneficiary with State authorities, but the record did not establish that the landowners had received the money before possession or promptly thereafter.
The State paid the award only after a substantial delay.
issues.conclusion: Justice Swatanter Kumar held that, where the prescribed advance compensation was not paid on time, the claimants were entitled to additional interest, applying the enhanced interest rate in the proviso to Section 34 from the relevant emergency-acquisition period until payment. He also held that interest was payable on the balance compensation from possession. The judges' broader disagreement was referred to a larger Bench.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Kumar read Sections 17(1), 17(3A), and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 harmoniously, treating the advance-payment obligation as requiring payment before possession and applying the interest protection in Section 34 to non-compliance. He also applied the principle that, where the law specifies no time for performance, payment must be made within a reasonable time.

predicates.emergency_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked an emergency procedure.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the land.
predicates.advance_compensation_received_before_pos: The landowners received the prescribed advance compensation before possession was taken.

issues.definition: In an emergency-acquisition case, if possession is taken before the landowners receive the prescribed advance compensation, Justice Kumar's view entitles the claimants to additional interest for delayed payment.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in challenging an emergency acquisition and completed development may disentitle a claimant to equitable relief that would undo the acquisition.
material_facts: The landowners challenged the acquisition more than two years after possession had been taken and did not satisfactorily explain the delay.
The acquired area had been developed and industrial plots had been allotted to third parties.
The award had been accepted by nearly all other affected owners, and substantial public and private resources had been invested in development.
issues.conclusion: Justice Swatanter Kumar held that the claimants were not entitled to equitable relief undoing the acquisition, given the unexplained delay, completed development, and reliance by others. Justice Ganguly also declined to restore the land in the circumstances, instead directing compensation to be assessed on a later valuation basis. The judges differed on the legal basis and remedy, and the matter was referred to a larger Bench.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Kumar applied equitable principles concerning delay and laches and relied on Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. L. Chandrasekaran and A.S. Naidu v. State of Tamil Nadu concerning the consequences of disturbing completed development and third-party interests. Justice Ganguly considered the completed development and third-party interests relevant to choosing compensation rather than restoration as the remedy.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_case: The proceeding challenges a compulsory acquisition and seeks relief that would undo it.
predicates.unexplained_delay_in_challenge: The landowner brought the challenge after substantial delay that was not adequately explained.
predicates.development_completed_with_third_party_i: The acquired land was developed and third parties obtained interests in it.

issues.definition: When an acquisition challenge is brought after unexplained delay and development has created third-party interests, relief undoing the acquisition is denied under Justice Kumar's view.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner whose emergency acquisition did not satisfy the advance-payment condition may receive compensation assessed by reference to a later valuation date when restoration is impracticable.
material_facts: The prescribed advance compensation was not paid before possession was taken, in Justice Ganguly's view making possession and vesting unlawful.
The acquired land had been transferred to the beneficiary, developed, and become subject to third-party interests.
Restoring the land was impracticable, and the claimants had filed a challenge seeking relief.
issues.conclusion: Justice Asok Kumar Ganguly directed that compensation be assessed using the value at the time the claimants filed their challenge, with a new award and liberty to challenge it. He did not direct restoration of the land because development and third-party interests made that impracticable. Justice Swatanter Kumar disagreed with the premise that non-payment invalidated the acquisition. The judges' divergent dispositions were referred to a larger Bench.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Ganguly relied on Sections 17(1), 17(2), and 17(3A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Article 300A, and the principle that possession taken contrary to a statutory condition precedent cannot effect vesting. He treated compensation based on a later valuation date as appropriate in the special circumstances where restoration was impracticable. Justice Kumar relied on the vesting scheme and the absence of a statutory power to revest land after possession.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_case: The proceeding challenges a compulsory acquisition and seeks relief concerning the acquired land.
predicates.advance_payment_condition_breached: The prescribed advance compensation was not paid to the landowners before possession was taken.
predicates.restoration_impracticable_due_to_develop: The land was developed or transferred so that restoring it to the landowners was impracticable.

issues.definition: When an acquisition challenge involves a breach of the advance-payment condition and development makes restoration impracticable, Justice Ganguly's view is that compensation may be assessed by reference to the later challenge date.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection of property requires emergency acquisition powers to comply with the statutory safeguards governing deprivation of property.
material_facts: The acquisition used emergency powers that dispensed with the landowners' opportunity to object before acquisition.
The landowners were not paid the prescribed advance compensation before possession was taken.
The relevant constitutional provision protects against deprivation of property except by authority of law, while property is no longer a fundamental right.
issues.conclusion: Justice Asok Kumar Ganguly held that the advance-payment safeguard gives effect to the constitutional protection of property and that taking possession without it violates that protection. Justice Swatanter Kumar held that the constitutional property right is not on the same footing as a fundamental right and that the statutory scheme balances individual and State interests. The judges differed, and the matter was referred to a larger Bench.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Ganguly relied on Article 300A and the due-process interpretation in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, together with Sections 17(1) and 17(3A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Justice Kumar relied on the deletion of Article 19(1)(f), the addition of Article 300A, and the statutory scheme, including Sections 17 and 11A, to conclude that the constitutional right to property should not be equated with a fundamental right.

predicates.emergency_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked an emergency procedure.
predicates.possession_taken_without_advance_payment: The acquiring authority took possession without first paying the prescribed advance compensation to the landowners.

issues.definition: In an emergency-acquisition case, if possession is taken without advance payment, Justice Ganguly's view requires compliance with the payment safeguard for deprivation of property to be constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: Conflicting opinions on the legal effect of non-payment in an emergency acquisition require referral to a larger Bench.
material_facts: The two judges reached conflicting conclusions about whether advance payment was a condition precedent to possession and vesting.
They also disagreed on whether non-payment invalidated the acquisition and on the appropriate relief.
issues.conclusion: The judges referred the matter to the Chief Justice of India for placement before a larger Bench to resolve their divergent views and answer the questions of law; the appeal was not conclusively disposed of by a majority ruling in this judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The judges expressly directed referral because their separate judgments diverged on the conclusions and legal questions. No statutory provision or earlier case was identified as the basis for this referral.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.separate_judgments_conflict_on_questions: The judges delivered separate judgments that reached conflicting conclusions on legal questions.

issues.definition: When a Supreme Court appeal produces conflicting separate judgments on legal questions, the matter is referred to a larger Bench.
